config.prompt: A fair die, rolled three times. What is the chance of at least one six, in percent?
config.why: 1 − (5/6)³ ≈ 0.42 — the complement rule turns 'at least one' into a single clean path instead of a pile of cases.
config.context: Complements always sum to 1: P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

activities.caption: file each claim with its hypothesis
activities.name: htHypSort

config.prompt: Which claims are defaults to be overturned, and which are what a result would establish?
buckets: a job for H₀ — the 'nothing' default
a job for H₁ — what a result would establish

items.label: the new timetable makes no difference

config.why: 'Nothing is going on' is usually precise and computable, while 'something is going on' is vague — surprise is computed against the precise claim, and the null is never proved, only survived.

activities.anchor: the friend's coin earns serious suspicion
activities.caption: one line of the coin test is wrong — click it
activities.name: htCoinSpot

config.prompt: One line of this worked test is wrong — click it:
lines: H₀: the coin is fair (p = 0.5); H₁: the coin is biased (p ≠ 0.5 — two-sided, since suspicion was flagged before knowing the direction).
α = 0.05 — the false-alarm rate tolerated, chosen before the flips.
P(exactly 9 heads in 10 fair flips) = C(10,9) × 0.5¹⁰ = 10/1024; P(10 heads) = 1/1024.
Verdict: 0.0215 < 0.05, so reject H₀ and report the effect honestly.
config.correction: The suspicion was two-sided, so the p-value is 2 × (10 + 1)/1024 = 22/1024 ≈ 0.0215 — both directions counted, which is exactly what line 5 compares against α.
config.why: The test never computes the probability that the coin is unfair — that would need a prior. It quantifies how embarrassing the data is for fairness.

activities.anchor: both flip that conditional or inflate it
activities.caption: the four misreadings — pair each with its defusal
activities.name: pvalMatch

config.prompt: Match each misreading to the honest reply:

pairs.left: “p is the probability H₀ is true”
pairs.right: No — it is computed assuming H₀; P(evidence | cause) and P(cause | evidence) came out 99% versus 16.7% on the disease tree
No — replication depends on the true effect size and the repeat study's power
No — the data did not clear the bar; the study may simply have been too small
No — the gap is noise-level trivial; α is a convention and p is a continuous measure of surprise

config.why: The ASA's 2016 statement catalogued exactly these errors: a p-value indicates how incompatible the data are with a specified model — it measures nothing else.

config.prompt: Testing 1,000 drug candidates of which 50 truly work, at α = 0.05 with 80% power: roughly how many false 'discoveries' do you expect?
config.why: 950 true nulls × 0.05 ≈ 48 false discoveries beside 50 × 0.8 = 40 true ones — over half the significant results are wrong, purely from base rates.
config.context: This is why multiple-comparisons discipline, Bonferroni's α/n, pre-registration and replication exist.

activities.caption: true or false — reading a p above the bar
activities.name: htSigJudge

statements.s: 'Not significant' proves the effect does not exist.
statements.why: A large, careful trial can return p = 0.2 for a small-but-real effect — the study may simply lack power.

statements.s: The confidence interval on the effect shows precisely what the study could and could not rule out.
statements.why: 'Somewhere between −0.1 and +0.9 points' converts the verdict into a quantitative statement.

statements.s: Absence of evidence is evidence of absence.
statements.why: The p-value only says the data did not clear the bar — the interval is what says what was actually excluded.

activities.caption: two kinds of significant — drag the divider
activities.name: htEffCompare

config.prompt: Both p-values cleared 0.05 — drag the divider:

before.label: significant but clinically trivial
before.text: a drug that lowers blood pressure by 0.1 mmHg — p = 0.01, n = 50,000 — is a 'so what?' once the effect size is in units that matter

after.label: significant and huge
after.text: pair every p with an effect size and a confidence interval — the previous lesson's error bar on it — and the two stories separate

config.why: A lone p-value under-reports its own story: one number about one comparison under one model.

activities.anchor: the exchange rate between the two errors
activities.caption: you set α before the data — walk three decisions
activities.name: htAlphaBranch

config.root: α is a priced decision, not a statistical constant. Walk the desk.

start.text: Screening a blood donation for a dangerous virus. What bar do you set?

choices.label: α very low, plus confirmatory testing
choices.feedback: A false negative contaminates the supply — the costs are asymmetric and catastrophic in one direction.

choices.label: 0.05 — the universal convention
choices.feedback: The convention is not a constant here; the price of each error decides.

screen.text: Next file: an A/B test of a button colour. What bar?

choices.label: 0.05 is generous — speed wins
choices.feedback: Both errors cost pennies; waiting costs more than either error does.

choices.label: α = 0.001 — buttons are safety-critical
choices.feedback: Overkill — the economics do not justify the width.

ab.text: Filed. And a comet-sampling spacecraft gets evidence standards so extreme that a false positive can never waste a billion-euro mission.

trap.text: Mispriced — reporting a single p-value without saying what each error would have cost reports the arithmetic while hiding the economics.

config.why: The significance level belongs to the decision, not the mathematics — blood, buttons and spacecraft set it differently.
